conventions: Each unit is a move of play: a repeatable action with an entry state, timed phases, an exit state and the three times a contest reads. tell_s is how long an opponent can see the move coming before it can no longer be changed; commits_s is how long it then holds the body to its course; recover_s is how long after it ends before the next quick action can start. A state is a posture (humanities/sport/state.py, POSTURES), a momentum (still; slow, up to the walking limit sqrt(g h); travelling) and the ball (held or free); 'same' keeps the entry's and 'any' takes every value. Durations, times and figures are expressions that vocabulary.physics() evaluates for one body, world and grip; a unit's let names are evaluated first, in order. A phase marked overlaps runs inside the flight it happens in and adds no time. Shapes are left to the whole-body round, which adds the athletic poses it needs to the pose library.
evidence: Moves drawn from court and field sports, athletics, gymnastics, cheerleading and the martial arts, and designed for the Moon from the envelope's mechanics. Durations and limits are physics screens of the envelope's closed forms with the assumptions stated in vocabulary.py, state.py and envelope.py; no move has been solved on the whole body, measured in low gravity or played.

families.going: Getting set, starting, travelling, turning and stopping
families.jumps: Leaving the floor and the arcs it commits to
families.contact: Pushes between players, a teammate's boost, falling and getting up

units.name: ready crouch
units.source: the ready position of court and field sports: basketball's defensive stance, a tennis player's split step, a goalkeeper's set
units.description: Feet wide, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet, the centre of mass lowered and held there, facing the play.
units.lunar: adapted: sinking into the crouch takes 0.47 s on the Moon against 0.23 s on Earth, since a body sinks no faster than g. Once held, the crouch is the quickest start a standing player has: a push sideways at 0.47 of g from the first instant, which carries the player 2 m aside in 1.95 s (Earth 0.89 s), and a jump with no dip.
checks: the descent no faster than g
the push inside the support and the grip

units.name: lean start
units.source: a sprinter's falling start; the first step of a walk
units.description: From standing upright, the body tips off its support toward where it is going, and the push grows with the lean.
units.lunar: adapted: from upright the body must tip before it can push, and gravity sets the pace: the first 0.1 m takes 0.88 s on the Moon against 0.36 s on Earth, and the first metre 2.1 s against 0.9 s. An upright player is a slow one.
checks: the inverted pendulum about the support's edge
the push at most the grip's

units.name: drop step
units.source: a sprinter's false step; basketball's drop step
units.description: One foot steps back behind the centre of mass toward the way the player will go, so the first push comes from behind at once.
units.lunar: native in its use: the step takes the muscles' quarter second on either world and puts the push behind the body at once, at 0.67 of g, so the first metre takes 1.53 s on the Moon against the lean's 2.14 s. The step saves 0.6 s on the Moon and 0.06 s on Earth, and it shows the direction a quarter second before the push.
checks: the push inside the split stance and the grip

units.name: shuffle
units.source: a defender's slide in basketball and handball; a fencer's footwork
units.description: Quick side steps with a foot always on the floor, the body level and facing the play.
units.lunar: adapted: a foot can stay on the floor only below about sqrt(g h), 1.2 m/s on the Moon against 3.0 m/s on Earth; faster, the body leaves the floor over the standing foot and the gait becomes a bound. Two metres aside take 2.3 s (Earth 0.96 s), with control at every moment.
checks: a foot down at every moment, so the speed stays under sqrt(g h)
the push at most the grip's

units.name: bounding run
units.source: the Apollo astronauts' lope and skip on the Moon; the dance's orbit run
units.description: Low running bounds, each stance a push and each flight a short glide; speed builds or bleeds stride by stride.
units.lunar: native: the lunar gait at speed. Each stance can change the travel by up to 1.1 m/s at a grip of 0.8 (0.7 at 0.5, 1.6 at 1.2; Earth 4.2), and over a stride the push averages the weight, so building or shedding 3 m/s takes 2.3 s and 3.5 m (Earth 0.38 s and 0.57 m), and a steady turn at 3 m/s needs a 6.9 m radius (Earth 1.2 m). A 5 cm bound flies 0.5 s, and the runner is held to its arc until the next stance.
checks: each stance's change within the grip on its vertical impulse
the stride's push averaging the weight

units.name: cut through a bounce
units.source: the cut of field and court sports (rugby's sidestep, basketball's crossover), rebuilt for the Moon
units.description: A higher bound lands on one foot and leaves in a new direction; the turn is paid for with the bounce's vertical impulse.
units.lunar: native: at speed a cut is a jump. Turning 45 degrees at 3 m/s needs a bounce of 0.42 m at a grip of 0.8 (1.27 m at 0.5, 0.15 m at 1.2), where an Earth stride turns it with no bounce at all. The higher bound into the cut shows a cut is coming 1.4 s ahead, though not which way, and the bound out of it holds the cutter as long.
checks: the change within the grip on the stance's vertical impulse (envelope.cut_bounce)

units.name: braking landing
units.source: landings in volleyball, parkour and the long jump
units.description: Coming down from a flight or a bound, the legs take the landing over a deep stroke and the floor's push takes the travel with it; what the landing leaves slides off.
units.lunar: adapted: a landing is where travel stops. Landing at 3 m/s with 2 m/s down sheds 2.1 m/s in the 0.4 s stance at a grip of 0.8 and slides the rest off in 0.7 s, stopping in 1.1 m (Earth 0.6 m, all in the stance); at a grip of 1.2 the stance takes it all. The push is 0.7 of an Earth body weight.
checks: the travel's change within the grip on the landing's vertical impulse (envelope.braking_landing)

units.name: pivot
units.source: basketball's pivot; a goalkeeper's turn to face
units.description: Turning the body to face a new direction on both feet, without travelling.
units.lunar: adapted: the feet's friction couple turns the body on gravity's clock: a quarter turn takes 0.45 s on the Moon against 0.19 s on Earth at a grip of 0.8, and a half turn 0.64 s against 0.26 s. A lunar player keeps facing the play and moves sideways or backward rather than turning to run.
checks: the turning moment within the feet's friction couple

units.name: standing jump
units.source: the countermovement jump of jump testing; a jump ball
units.description: From standing upright, the body sinks into a dip and drives up off both feet.
units.lunar: adapted: a jump sinks only as deep as its height needs. A 1 m rise, which lifts the hands to 3.25 m, needs a 5 cm dip and leaves the floor 0.38 s after the jumper starts, then holds the player 2.2 s in its arc. The highest jump, 2.86 m, sinks 0.28 m and shows itself 0.87 s ahead, where Earth's best (0.29 m) shows itself 0.62 s ahead.
checks: the dip no faster than g
the take-off within the force-velocity profile

units.name: jump from the crouch
units.source: the squat jump of jump testing; a volleyball blocker's jump from a held crouch
units.description: From the held ready crouch, the legs drive straight up with no dip first.
units.lunar: native in its use: from a held crouch the legs need no dip up to a 2.1 m rise, so a 1 m jump leaves the floor 0.17 s after the decision, less than a reaction time. Holding the crouch costs a quarter of the full jump's height.
checks: the take-off within the force-velocity profile over the crouch's shorter push

units.name: rebound jump
units.source: the drop jump of plyometrics; a basketball rebound; the dance's grand jeté out of a stride
units.description: Out of a landing or a stride, the legs take the coming down as their dip and drive up again at once.
units.lunar: adapted: out of a landing or a stride the take-off needs no dip, so the only notice is the arc the jumper is already on. A 1 m rebound holds the player 2.2 s; Earth's best rebound holds 0.5 s.
checks: the take-off within the force-velocity profile
the landing's stroke as the countermovement

units.name: side hop
units.source: a goalkeeper's dive; a lateral hop in tennis and volleyball
units.description: From the ready crouch, a push off the far foot throws the body sideways and up in one arc.
units.lunar: adapted: the stance's geometry limits the sideways push to 0.47 of the upward one, so a 0.3 m hop moves the player 0.56 m in a 1.2 s arc, 1.5 s in all (Earth 0.41 m in 0.64 s). The ready crouch's push covers the same 0.56 m in 1.1 s with a foot always down, so on the Moon a hop buys no ground, only height.
checks: the push's line inside the stance and the grip (envelope.jumps, lateral hop)

units.name: running leap
units.source: the long jump; the dance's grand jeté
units.description: Out of a bound, one stance sends the body into a long arc that keeps its speed.
units.lunar: native: a 0.5 m rise at 3 m/s carries the player 4.7 m in a 1.6 s arc (Earth 1.5 m in 0.5 s). The arc is the leap's whole plan, readable from its take-off.
checks: the take-off within the force-velocity profile

units.name: chest pass
units.source: basketball's and netball's two-handed chest pass
units.description: Both hands push the ball from the chest, close to the centre of mass, with the feet under the body.
units.lunar: native in its use: pushed from the chest, close to the centre of mass, a pass turns the thrower little, so feet under the body hold a release of 9.9 m/s on the Moon where an overhand throw from the same stance holds 3.0 (the larger body 15.9 and 4.3); on Earth both reach the arm's own limit. The chest pass is the standing player's pass.
checks: the throw's moment within the floor's push at the support's edge
the hand force within the grip

units.name: throw from a split stance
units.source: handball's and baseball's overhand throws; the javelin's last stride
units.description: With the rear foot set well behind the centre of mass, the arm winds up and throws overhand; the rear foot holds the throw's push.
units.lunar: adapted: the rear foot 0.5 m behind the centre of mass holds an overhand release of 14.9 m/s on the Moon (the larger body reaches the arm's 20), so a hard throw starts from a step back, which shows it a quarter second or more ahead.
checks: the throw's moment within the floor's push at the rear foot
the hand force within the grip

units.name: throw into a landing
units.source: handball's jump shot released at the landing; a bowler's front-foot landing in cricket
units.description: The throw is timed into the landing's stance, when the floor pushes hardest.
units.lunar: native: the floor pushes hardest in a landing, 0.96 of an Earth body weight for 2.5 m/s down over 0.4 m, and that push holds an overhand release of 17.3 m/s. The landing's time and place are set at take-off, so an opponent can read the throw's moment from the arc.
checks: the throw's moment within the landing's push at the support's edge

units.name: pass in the air
units.source: volleyball's set and attack; handball's jump pass
units.description: Aloft, the hands release the ball; with no floor to hold the push, the throw's reaction turns the body.
units.lunar: native: with no floor, the ball's push turns the thrower. A 10 m/s release overhead leaves enough spin to turn the body 31 degrees by the landing laid out and 123 degrees tucked (Earth 5 and 20), so a pass in the air goes from the chest or goes softly, or is paid for in the landing.
checks: the release's angular momentum carried to the landing

units.name: catch
units.source: every ball game's catch, giving with the ball
units.description: The hands meet the ball and give with it, taking its momentum over the give.
units.lunar: adapted: a catch takes the ball's momentum as a throw gives it. Feet under, a 0.15 s give holds a 9.9 m/s ball at the chest and 3.0 m/s overhead, and overhead from a split stance 14.9 m/s; a 0.3 s give doubles each, up to the arm's 20 m/s. Balls in the design air arrive at 4-6 m/s.

figures.chest_holds_m_s: hold_m_s(fore_aft, chest_lever, m * g, ball_kg, give_s)
figures.overhead_holds_m_s: hold_m_s(fore_aft, lever, m * g, ball_kg, give_s)
figures.split_overhead_holds_m_s: hold_m_s(split, lever, m * g, ball_kg, give_s)

checks: the catch's moment within the floor's push, as a throw's in reverse

units.name: scoop from the floor
units.source: an infielder's ground ball; a goalkeeper's gather
units.description: The body sinks until the hands reach the floor, gathers the ball and rises back into the crouch.
units.lunar: adapted: reaching the floor takes 0.78 s on the Moon against 0.39 s on Earth, and rising back into the crouch 0.64 s against 0.37 s. Low balls are slow balls.
checks: the descent no faster than g
the rise stopping no faster than g

units.name: kick
units.source: football's instep kick; a rugby punt
units.description: The kicking leg winds back and swings through the ball while the standing foot holds what it can of the turn.
units.lunar: adapted: the swing keeps Earth's tempo and sends a football off at about 16 m/s on either world, but the standing foot holds the ball's reaction about the body at a sixth of Earth's moment, so the kicker takes 0.59 s to settle, against Earth's 0.10 s.
checks: the ball's reaction about the centre of mass within the standing foot's moment

units.name: shove
units.source: a rugby hand-off; a basketball box-out; sumo's push
units.description: Both hands push an opponent from a split stance, the body leaning into the push.
units.lunar: native in its limit: the push leans the pusher back over the rear foot, so the lean limits it before the grip does, to 0.43 of the pusher's weight on either world: 39 N on the Moon against 234 N on Earth, on any of the floors. A deeper lean pushes harder, and a lean builds on gravity's clock.
checks: the push within the pusher's grip and the lean over the rear foot

units.name: brace
units.source: a scrum's set in rugby; a lineman's stance; a judoka's base
units.description: Turning into the push with a foot back and the weight leaning into it, to take a shove or a bump.
units.lunar: adapted: facing the push with a foot back, a player holds 0.43 of their weight (39 N on the Moon); squared up in the wide crouch with the feet side by side, only 0.09 (7.8 N); turned side-on, the wide stance along the push, 0.30 (27 N). A lunar player meets contact with a foot back or turned, and a quarter turn takes 0.45 s.
checks: the held push within the grip and the lean over the rear foot

units.name: teammate's boost
units.source: the tosses of cheerleading and acrobatic gymnastics; a rugby lineout lift
units.description: A teammate's two-arm push under the flyer's foot or seat throws the flyer up.
units.lunar: native: a teammate's two-arm push throws a 55 kg player 1.75 m up for 2.9 s (an 80 kg player 1.0 m), where on Earth the same push lifts no one. The set and the push show the boost 0.75 s ahead.
checks: the push against the flyer's weight over the arms' stroke (envelope.contact, toss)

units.name: fall and rise
units.source: judo's breakfall and get-up; a goalkeeper's recovery
units.description: Knocked off balance, the body topples, takes the floor on its hands and side, and gets up into the crouch.
units.lunar: adapted: a topple from 5 degrees takes 2.0 s to reach 35 degrees (Earth 0.8 s), time the faller can use to catch it with a step, and the whole fall and rise takes 3.5 s (Earth 1.7 s).
checks: the topple as an inverted pendulum
the rise stopping no faster than g
